exercise training results in an up-regulation of basal heat shock protein and antioxidant protein content of skeletal muscles in humans.
exercise training results in a significant increase in the resting levels of Hsp60, alphaB-crystallin and MnSOD in human skeletal muscle.

exercise training increases the basal content of heat shock proteins and antioxidant enzymes in human skeletal muscle, which may serve to protect the muscle from the deleterious effects of exercise and/or aging.

trained men have higher levels of heat shock proteins and superoxide dismutases in skeletal muscle.

The main takeaway from our work is that

exercise training can increase the content of heat shock and oxidative stress proteins in skeletal muscle, which may function to maintain homeostatic balance in the muscle cell during the stress of training.

the trained state is characterized by increased levels of HSPs and antioxidant proteins, but that the stress response of trained human muscle to exercise is not characterized by a further increase in these protective proteins.
the exercise-induced heat shock response may not occur in trained individuals, and that trained individuals may be better able to maintain cellular homeostasis during exercise.
